newsitem.title: USA: GM market share quest may be hurt by weak yen.
newsitem.headline: GM market share quest may be hurt by weak yen.

text.p: General Motors Corp.'s quest to regain lost market share this year could run in to trouble if the Japanese yen continues to fall against the dollar, GM's North American chief said Wednesday.

G. Richard Wagoner, president of GM's North American Operations, complained to reporters at the Chicago auto show that U.S. market share gains by Toyota Motor Corp. and other Japanese automakers in January were due in large measure to a yen that he said is being deliberately weakened by efforts of the Japanese government.
He said weak yen could "erode the base" of GM's cost reductions and operational improvements over time.

On Wednesday, the dollar soared to a four-year high against the yen, climbing in New York to 123.85 yen, its highest since it hit 124.33 yen during the week of Feb. 14, 1993. That compares with about 80 yen to the dollar in April 1995.

"After five years of slow growth, the (Japanese) Ministry of Finance is reverting to its old tricks -- seeking a competitive devaluation to promote exports," Wagoner said. "I guess structural reform, which is the real answer to Japan's economic problems, is simply too difficult to implement."

In January, Asian automakers increased their share of the U.S. market by 3.4 percentage points, to 25.3 percent, largely at the expense of the Big Three U.S. automakers, who lost 3.8 points as a group.
Toyota scored the biggest gain, lifting its U.S. market share by 3.1 percentage points to 9.8 percent.
GM's share, on the other hand, sank nearly two points to 30.1 percent, with sales down 1 percent.

The auto giant has vowed to reverse its long-term slide in market share this year with the introduction of 15 new car and truck models. Wagoner said launches of new models are currently progressing on or ahead of schedule, and GM expected to begin advertising soon for its a new line of minivans and the new Chevrolet Malibu mid-size car.

"For '97, we're quite confident in our ability to gain share, but I'd have to say here that the yen is becoming more of a factor every day than it should be," Wagoner said, adding that GM cannot easily accelerate its cost cutting efforts further.

Toyota officials denied on Wednesday that the company's January U.S. market share gains are a windfall from the weaker yen. Rather, they are the result of introductions of new, lower-cost models that are a hit with consumers, such as the Camry sedan, the Lexus ES300 luxury car, and the 4-Runner sport utility vehicle.

"You didn't hear us complaining when it was 85 yen to the dollar," said James Olson, Toyota Motor Sales USA's senior vice president for external affairs. "We just hunkered down and cut our costs. "I'd suggest to (U.S. automakers) that they do the same."

Olson also said the Japanese government is not manipulating the yen. He said he believes the currency is trading at its current level because of the strength in the U.S. economy and economic weakness in Japan. "Japan's economy is in trouble, and the currency reflects that."
He added that Toyota believes the exchange rate is more appropriate at about 110 yen to the dollar.
